primitives.name: Determinant Circuit
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Circuit equation: det M[(a,a_1,...,a_r),(s*,s_1,...,s_r)] = 0 solved for the missing entry; first-order weight: σ_i ← 1/|det A_0 + det A_1| + |det A_0|/(det A_0 - det A_1)2, w_i ← σ_i^{-2}, m* ← (Σ w_i m_i)/(Σ w_i).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'M': 'r+1 × r+1 submatrix of the athlete-event performance matrix', 'a': 'target athlete index', 's*': 'target event distance', 'a_i': 'indices of r neighboring athletes', 's_i': 'distances of r neighboring events', 'm*': 'predicted performance (time)', 'w_i': 'weight for neighbor i', 'σ_i': 'estimated standard deviation of prediction error', 'A_0, A_1': ' auxiliary matrices used in weight computation'}
primitives.assumptions: Low-rank assumption: performance matrix has rank r; Local independence: missing entries depend only on nearby athletes and events; Determinantal structure: the missing entry satisfies a polynomial equation derived from a principal minor.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity when determinants vanish (|det A_0| ≈ |det A_1|) → infinite variance weights; High-dimensional regime (r large) → numerical instability.

layer2.mapping: The determinant circuit implements a maximum-likelihood imputation under a multivariate Gaussian latent factor model with isotropic noise. It corresponds to a kernel regression with a Gaussian process prior over rows/columns, where the covariance is defined via the Grassmannian distance between r-planes spanned by neighboring athletes/events.
layer2.telemetry: Validation: compare imputed values against held-out test sets; diagnostic: check whether the empirical distribution of imputed errors follows the predicted σ_i.

primitives.name: Local Low-Rank Matrix Completion
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Second stage: impute all missing entries with LMC rank 3, then SVD → universal components f_1,f_2,f_3 (right singular vectors) and per-athlete three-number summary (λ_1,λ_2,λ_3) from left singular vectors.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'Y': 'sparse athlete-event performance matrix', 'U_k, V_k': 'left/right singular vectors (k=3)', 'Σ_k': 'diagonal matrix of top singular values', 'λ_i': 'singular values interpreted as scaling factors for individual performance', 'f_i(s)': 'basis functions encoding event dependence'}
primitives.assumptions: The underlying true matrix has approximately low rank (k << min(#athletes, #events)); Missing-at-random (MAR) given the low-rank structure; Observations are noisy perturbations of the low-rank signal.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Overfitting when k exceeds the effective rank; Slow convergence when singular values decay too slowly, making the low-rank approximation less accurate.

layer2.mapping: LMC is equivalent to applying a nuclear-norm regularized maximum-likelihood estimator under a Gaussian observation model. The resulting predictor is a linear combination of the top k right singular vectors, weighted by the corresponding left singular values and the observed data.
layer2.telemetry: Monitor the gap between the observed and reconstructed Frobenius norm on a validation set; check whether the recovered singular vectors exhibit meaningful biological/physical patterns.

primitives.name: Bagged Kernel Regression
primitives.verbatim_quote: - k for k-NN tuned from {1,5,20} minimizing OOS RMSE on 5×50 validation points; bagged variants weight via Gaussian RBF kernel exp(γΔΔT), γ ∈ {-0.001,-0.01,-0.1,-1,-10} selected by CV.
primitives.latex: f(x^*) = \frac{\sum_{i \in N_k(x^*)} w_i f(x_i)}{\sum_{i \in N_k(x^*)} w_i}, \quad w_i = \exp\left(-\gamma \Delta x_i^2\right)
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'x^*': 'query point (athlete-event)', 'x_i': 'neighbors', 'N_k': 'k-nearest neighbors', 'γ': 'bandwidth parameter controlling kernel width', 'Δx_i': 'distance between query and neighbor', 'w_i': 'Gaussian kernel weight'}
primitives.assumptions: Smoothness: nearby inputs have similar outputs; Local linearity may hold; The choice of k and γ balances bias (under-smoothing) versus variance (over-smoothing).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Under-smoothing (k small, γ large) leads to high variance; Over-smoothing (k large, γ small) introduces bias, especially near boundaries or regions with sparse data.

layer2.mapping: Bagging reduces variance by averaging multiple k-NN models trained on bootstrap samples. The Gaussian RBF kernel can be viewed as a non-parametric estimate of the posterior mean under a Gaussian process with a squared-exponential covariance function. The bandwidth γ controls the length scale of this kernel.
layer2.telemetry: Track out-of-sample RMSE as a function of γ and k; use cross-validation to select the optimal pair; examine the stability of predictions across different bootstrap replicates.

primitives.name: Synthetic Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: 2): log(t) = λ_1 f_1(s) + λ_2 f_2(s) + λ_3 f_3(s) + η(s), η stationary zero-mean Gaussian white noise; plausible Std(η) = 0.01.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'t': 'performance time', 'a': 'athlete identifier', 's': 'event descriptor (e.g., distance)', 'λ_i': 'per-athlete scaling coefficients', 'f_i(s)': 'global basis functions capturing event effects', 'η(s)': 'event-specific random noise with standard deviation σ = 0.01'}
primitives.assumptions: Additive noise: the observed time is the sum of a deterministic trend and independent Gaussian noise; Homoskedasticity: the noise variance is constant across all events; Independence: noise at different events is uncorrelated.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When σ becomes too large, the model loses predictive power; When σ approaches zero, the model becomes overly rigid and prone to overfitting.

layer2.mapping: This synthetic model is a special case of a generalized additive model (GAM) with fixed smooth terms. It can also be interpreted as a Bayesian linear regression with a conjugate Gaussian prior on the coefficients, where the prior precision is set to ensure that the posterior mean shrinks towards the origin.
layer2.telemetry: Compare the synthetic predictions against actual performance data; compute the residual standard deviation and assess whether it follows a normal distribution; evaluate the predictive accuracy using cross-validation.
